screen.substantive_issue: Whether the tenant had sub-let or parted with the shop premises to Sohan Singh where they lived as husband and wife and he principally ran the chemist business there.

issue_refs.quote: The simple question which had to be determined in the case was whether having regard to the fact that the appellant and Sohan Singh were living as husband and wife, it was open to draw, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, the factual inference that the wife had sub-let the premises to her husband.

application_refs.quote: If two persons live together in a house as husband and wife and one of them who owns the house allows the other to carry on business in a part of it,it will be in the absence of any other evidence, a rash inference to draw that the owner has let out that part of the premises.
These provisions evidently have no application to the facts of the present case.
In the present case the respondent produced no evidence to show such sub-letting in spite of the appellant's denial in the written statement of any sub-letting.

The evidence was clear namely, that to the knowledge of the respondent, the appel- lant and Sohan Singh were living as husband and wife and from the day the rent note was passed by the appellant in 1959 a Chemist's shop was opened in the premises which was run principally by Sohan Singh but occasionally by the appellant also.

issue_refs.quote: Assuming that the bona fide requirement of the landlord is established, the landlord must still prove that the premises had been let for residential purposes.
The fundamental question in respect of residential premises is whether the landlord had consented to the user of the premises for any other purpose, albeit incidentally.

application_refs.quote: There is no substance in the contention that the landlord was unaware that the premises had been used for lodging foreign students.

In the present case, it is not disputed that the premises had been let for residential purposes, but it is also beyond doubt that to the knowledge of the landlord the premises have been regularly used by the tenant not only for her own residence but also for her foreign guests.
At no time did the landlord object to the user of the premises by the appellant for such purpose.

The continued user of the building ever since 1961 for the purpose of lodging paying guests shows that the respondent-landlord and her father have not only been aware of such user of the building, but have also impliedly consented to such user.
The evidence on record leaves no doubt that the premises have been regularly used by the appellant as a boarding house and not as a private 480 residence in the ordinary acceptation of the term.

screen.substantive_issue: Whether rent note Exhibit RW 4/7 constituted the required written landlord consent and written notice for the sub-tenancy involving Dewan Chand Gupta and Kirori Mal.

issue_refs.quote: The important document in this regard is Exhibit Rw 4/7. The interpretation of this document will tilt the issue.

application_refs.quote: Admittedly, in this case except the document exhibit Rw 4/7 no other written notice of creation of sub-tenancy was given nor there is any other written document evidencing the consent of the landlord admitting the sub tenancy.

The recital of Exhibit Rw 4/7 shows that when Onkar Nath was taken as a tenant in the premises in question by the then owner/landlord Shri InderNarain, S/Shri Dewan Chand Gupta, Pleader and Kirori Mal were already occupying the premises in question.
It shows the landlord Inder Narain gave his consent in writing to Onkar Nath to the creation to sub-tenancy in favour of Dewan Chand and Kirori Mal.
The landlord when became signatory to Exhibit Rw 4/7 it tantamount to having given his consent of sub-letting. It also shows notice in writing of sub-tenancy in respect of the above premises.
Exhibit Rw 4/7 amply proves that the landlord gave his consent in writing to the sub-letting and notice of the creation of sub-tenancy duly served on the landlord.
Since this Court is of the view that the document Exhibit RW4/7 is a written consent to the landlord/owner and a notice of creation of subtenancy, hence appeal must fail.

Current Advertising and Marketing, it had served its purpose and exhausted itself when the firm was dissolved and instead a company by the name of M/s. Current Advertising (P) Ltd. The eviction petition of the petitioners on the said ground is allowed.

issue_refs.quote: The impugned judgment had reversed this finding noting that a ground of subletting under cite12†Section 14(1)(b) of the DRCA has not been made out.

For the purpose of clause (b) of the proviso to sub-section (1), any premises which have been let for being used for the purposes of business or profession shall be deemed to have been sub-let by the tenant, if the Controller is satisfied that the tenant without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord has, after the 16th day of August, 1958, allowed any person to occupy the whole or any part of the premises ostensibly on the ground that such person is a partner of the tenant in the business or profession but really for the purpose of sub-letting such premises to that person.

application_refs.quote: In this scenario the RCT had correctly appreciated the evidence adduced; it is clear that the son-in-law has come to Delhi to assist his father-in-law in his business in the shop; both were residing in the same premises; because the father-in-law has become very old and because of his old age and weak eyesight he could not come regularly to his shop; his wife Sumitra Devi was opening and closing the shop with her son-in-law; she was also sitting in the shop; Ex.AW-3/13 was in fact not a sham document;

screen.substantive_issue: Whether the landlords proved that M/s Gargson was the proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta rather than Shri Arun Kumar Garg, and that M/s Gargson Autoplast was unauthorizedly inducted as a subtenant or given possession of the tenanted shop.

issue_refs.quote: What is to be seen is as to whether the appellants have been able to establish that M/s Gargson was sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta and not of Shri Arun Kumar Garg and as to whether the appellants have been able to establish that M/s Gargson Autoplast was unauthorizedly inducted as subtenant or was parted with possession of the tenanted shop.

application_refs.quote: In the said document Ex. PW1/2, receipt of rent from M/s Gargson is shown, but there is not even a whisper that M/s Gargson is the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta.

Further, according to PW1, at the time of inception of tenancy, he was aged approximately six years and terms of tenancy were not settled in his presence, so even his oral testimony that the tenant inducted into the tenanted premises was M/s Gargson the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta is not believable.
it does not show that M/s Gargson sublet or parted with possession of the tenanted premises to M/s Gargson Autoplast.

Besides, the burden of proof was on the appellants to establish that the tenant inducted by their predecessor into the tenanted premises was the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta and not of Shri Arun Kumar Garg and that the said sole proprietorship concern of Shri Om Prakash Gupta had sublet or parted with possession of the tenanted shop to the sole proprietorship concern of Shri Arun Kumar Garg, both of which aspects could not be proved by the appellants during trial.

Therefore, I am unable to find any infirmity in the impugned order and judgment dated 05.05.2018 so far as the dismissal of petition on the ground stipulated under Section 14(1)(b) Delhi Rent Control Act is concerned.

screen.substantive_issue: Whether the tenant had parted with possession of or assigned the demised shop to his brother Bhagwan Dass, notwithstanding the defence that the brother merely helped or worked as an employee.

issue_refs.quote: In such circumstances, an inference can certainly be drawn that respondent has parted with the possession and assigned the premises to his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass. Initial onus, thus, stands discharged.

application_refs.quote: From the pleadings and evidence, it stands established that the shop in question is being operated and managed by respondent's brother Sh. Ghyamshyam Dass. He opens the shop; he closes the shop and deals with the customers. He possesses the key of the premises.
In the aforesaid facts and circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that respondent cannot be said to be in possession of the demised premises.

In such circumstances, an inference can certainly be drawn that respondent has parted with the possession and assigned the premises to his brother Sh. Bhagwan Dass. Initial onus, thus, stands discharged.
However, the vouchers or the proof of salary or payment register does not establish his defence.

This Court is of the opinion that in face of such patent facts, the trial court committed a grave error in not lifting the viel and seeing that it is a smokescreen created by the brothers, of a relationship of employer and employee to conceal the arrangement of assignment/ sub letting.
this Court is of the opinion that the trial court did not appreciate the legal and factual position correctly and committed a grave error in rejecting the landlord's case U/s 14(1)(b) of DRC Act.

independent_rule_leads.quote: Sub-tenancy or sub-letting comes into existence when the tenant gives up possession of the tenanted accommodation, wholly or in part, and puts another person in exclusive possession thereof.

Since payment of rent or monetary consideration may have been made secretly, the law does not require such payment to be proved by affirmative evidence and the Court is permitted to draw its own inference upon the facts of the case.
once landlord has established presence of stranger in tenancy premises, onus shifts on tenant to explain his presence.

screen.substantive_issue: Whether the respondents' arrangement with DTTDC, described by them as a licence on monthly commission, in fact amounted to subletting, assignment or parting with possession under Section 14(1)(b), including whether legal possession/control remained with the respondents and whether written consent existed.

issue_refs.quote: the respondents, being tenants under the applicant, have sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of the premises in favour of some other person.

application_refs.quote: it is found that the suit premises was given by the respondents to the DTTDC department in the year 1985. It is also found on the basis of admission of RW-1 during his cross-examination that respondents never took any permission from the landlord for the wine business to be done by the DTTDC in the suit premises before giving the same to DTTDC.

the business in the suit premises was a partnership business and he was not aware about the sale and purchase and business account of the wine business, as the same was looked after and managed by DTTDC

there is no partnership exist between the respondents and DTTDC, as there is no document filed by the respondents to substantiate the defence that they are partners. Therefore, on the basis of material especially on the basis of cross-examination of RW-1 it can be said that shop was not let out on commission basis rather on rent with DTTDC.

the document Ex.RW1/1 i.e. licence agreement does not contain even a single whisper that the respondents would retain legal possession over the suit property. In the case in hand, as the respondents are not able to discharge the onus that they have legal control or possession of the rented premises with them, therefore, it is presumed that DTTDC has exclusive possession over the suit property either sub-tenant or an assignee.

Further, in the document Ex.RW1/1, it is nowhere mentioned that the respondents have taken prior permission from the father of the petitioner regarding giving of the property to the DTTDC. In the light of the abovesaid discussion, the ground of eviction u/s. 14(1) (b) of DRC Act stands proved against the respondents.

independent_rule_leads.quote: (b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

Parting with possession means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession had been given by the lease. User by other person is not parting with possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself.
the onus to prove subletting is on the landlord and if he establishes parting of with the possession in favour of a third party, the onus would shift to the tenant to explain.

the use of premises by another is not sufficient to attract the provisions of clause (b) of proviso to sub-section (1) of section 14 of Act 59 of 1958 so long the legal possession is retained by the tenant.
as long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself there is no parting with possession in terms of section 14(1) (b) of the Act.
